Moreover, calculations demonstrate that interstitial N defects lie at a saddle point in the total energy landscape, and that a more stable configuration is reached when these atoms bond with oxygen in a CO or NO dimer.  Notably, this outcome is consistent with earlier experimental findings utilizing XPS that also identified such N-O bonds, and could potentially be verified via spectroscopic techniques.  Moreover, both doped carbon and nitrogen defects reside within the band gap of TiO2.  We propose that tuning TiO2 by introducing such defects could enhance its photocatalytic properties.

This letter describes the inspiration and an analytical method for detecting the production of top-quark pairs in the Large Hadron Collider through the identification of protons emitted at the front end. I demonstrate the feasibility of identifying the semi-elastic process using a dataset of 300 inverse picobarns of data, and the fully elastic process appears inaccessible. Furthermore, I illustrate that utilizing forward proton tags enables limits on certain rare top-quark decays such as $t\rightarrow u\gamma$ and $t\rightarrow c\gamma$ which would significantly surpass the current world records, with limits on branching ratios of $<0.39\cdot10^{-5}$ and $<0.97\cdot10^{-5}$, respectively.

Observations of the intra-cluster medium with X-rays offer a rich understanding of galaxy clusters' dynamics. Maintaining equilibrium within the ICM is partially achieved by non-thermal pressure and the dissipation of turbulent energy. X-ray emission line mapping, essential for studying ICM turbulence, is complicated by the lack of high-resolution spectroscopy. Future X-ray detectors like the X-IFU on Athena will enable thorough investigations of ICM turbulence across multiple scales. Crucial metrics for such studies include line shift and broadening maps, as well as the second-order structure function. When analyzed with proper techniques, these metrics can provide reliable estimates despite potential systematic errors. Based on simulated observations with the X-IFU, we evaluate the precision of structure function measurements as a function of spatial scale, temperature, and electron density. Our analysis flags potential uncertainties that researchers must be aware of when interpreting their data: below a certain threshold, the broadening's intrinsic variance can mask the effect of turbulence on structure functions; at larger scales, the broadening's variance becomes insufficient to accurately determine structure functions in a meaningful way; and in areas with exceptionally high temperatures or densities, the estimated structure function can be biased due to thermal motions. These limitations will need to be considered in upcoming Athena missions like the Athena X-IFU POC and the full Athena mission.

In 1993, Erdos and Galvin pioneered upper density problems within Ramsey theory, specifically the problem of identifying the highest $\lambda$ value such that in every two-edge coloring of the complete infinite graph, there exists an infinitely large, monochromatically colored subgraph resembling $F$ with an upper density of at least $\lambda$. We expand upon this research by providing a lower bound for this $\lambda$ value, with specific cases where the lower bound is equal to existing upper bounds for structures like cliques and odd cycles, and a $1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}$ value for triangles that surpasses the former record of 3/5.

Located at the heart of the Milky Way lies the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ), a distinct ring-like formation, where analysis of the 870 $\mu$m continuum map from ATLASGAL, obtained via the APEX Telescope Large Area Survey of the Galaxy, revealed notable anisotropy in gas density within this area using a two-dimensional correlation function. By identifying the critical angle $\theta_{\rm half}$ and anisotropy parameter $A\equiv \frac{\pi}{4\theta_{\rm half}}-1$, it was determined that gas density in the CMZ is significantly influenced by anisotropic spatial patterns at a scale of approximately 100 parsecs. These patterns decrease in anisotropic influence as the scale diminishes to about 10 parsecs. Our research offers a quantitative assessment of the anisotropic structure in gas within the CMZ and provides a method for comparing similar regions in various areas of the galaxy.

This paper introduces a groundbreaking method to identify Bell's Palsy solely by analyzing a person's eye movements in a video. We have observed that patients with Bell's Palsy encounter difficulty blinking their afflicted eye, creating a noticeable disparity in blinking patterns between the two eyes. Building on existing research, our work exclusively focuses on eye movements rather than entire facial images. This unique approach ensures individuals' anonymity and facilitates the interpretability of AI-driven conclusions. We have devised a novel metric called blink similarity, quantifying the similarity between blinking patterns, and successfully demonstrated its reliability through rigorous experiments requiring minimal labeled data. Notably, our eye-centric system offers enhanced efficiency and user-friendliness when compared to conventional methods.

Our analysis highlights the benefits of using qudits instead of qubits in scalar Quantum Electrodynamics in $(1+1)$d, specifically regarding their tolerance to errors. When measuring the mass gap using an out-of-time correlator as noise increases from both amplitude damping and Pauli channels, our findings reveal that simulations utilizing qutrits can handle up to 10 to 100 times more gate noise than their qubit-based counterparts for the same mass determination error. Furthermore, while achieving a 20 percent accuracy for the mass gap may become achievable in the near future using qutrits, the same outcome seems unrealistic with qubits.

Research indicates that positrons are efficiently produced through interactions between intense lasers and solid materials, specifically within the context of strong-field quantum electrodynamics. However, the polarization properties of these positrons remain unknown, hindering potential uses. Our study utilizes particle-in-cell simulations accounting for the polarization of photons and the spin of electrons and positrons to analyze the effects of an extremely intense linearly polarized laser on a thin, micrometer-scale target pre-heated by a thin layer of plasma. The results show that, when the number of generated positrons becomes substantial at intensities exceeding 10 to the power of 24 Watts per square centimeter, the produced positrons exhibit notable polarization properties. In fact, the polarization of the positrons can reach over thirty percent, with an accumulated charge exceeding 30 nanocoulombs, emitted with an enormous intensity of ten to the power of 12 per unit steradian. The degree of polarization is influenced by the angle of the emitted particles and their corresponding energies. In particular, the polarization is maximized at certain angles and reaches levels as high as sixty percent, primarily due to the unique interaction between the positrons and the intense laser fields within the overdense plasma. The occurrence of positron polarization is relatively robust, thereby likely manifesting in experiments using high-power lasers interacting with dense targets, with potential for a wide range of applications.

Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible diameter is defined as the minimum number n, such that any element of G can be expressed as the product of up to n elements from S. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed-sized generating set, and it demonstrates that these groups have a significant abelian subgroup close to their highest order, making up a substantial fraction of the group's total size. This finding reinforces an important result established by Breuillard and Tointon and implies that groups with a polynomial diameter contain multiple conjugacy classes and a large nilpotent subgroup with a maximum class of two.

This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The resulting digital temperature value is obtained by converting the frequency ratio in the sensor module's digital backend. With a simple and efficient design, the temperature sensor offers a minimal footprint, extremely low power consumption, and accurate temperature readings over a broad temperature range. Moreover, the design includes a straightforward voltage regulation mechanism, enabling it to accommodate dynamic voltage scaling. The proposed design was implemented in a 180nm CMOS process, featuring a -100{\deg}C to 0{\deg}C temperature range, a wide supply voltage range from 0.6V to 1.8V, and an incredibly compact silicon area of 0.021$mm^2$. Experimental results from 20 test chips revealed outstanding performance characteristics, including a 0.24{\deg}C resolution, a 1.4{\deg}C maximum inaccuracy, a 1.5kHz conversion rate, and an energy per conversion of 1.06nJ at 30{\deg}C.

Long-lasting stability in the magnetic fields of Ap-stars, white dwarfs, and neutron stars has been observed but the exact stellar interior conditions responsible are still the focus of ongoing research. Studies have revealed that magnetic fields purely in the toroidal or poloidal configurations inevitably succumb to instability. In contrast, numerical simulations have consistently shown stability in the axisymmetric configurations of the magnetic fields found within non-turbulent stellar interiors. These stable configurations consist of intertwined toroidal and poloidal components resembling a twisted torus. Prior studies have identified rough limits to the ratio of the toroidal and poloidal magnetic energy. In order to define the conditions necessary for these stable configurations, we ran three-dimensional simulations utilizing the Pencil Code for non-rotating stars experiencing viscosity-driven dissipation. Our simulations were performed for both barotropic stars with constant specific entropy and stably stratified stars, while varying parameters including the level of stable stratification and magnetic energy in each component, confirming existing predictions for the stability boundaries.

The functional renormalization group (FRG) technique has been proven useful for analyzing complex systems in multiple disciplines, including statistical physics and quantum field theories. Our research seeks to accelerate FRG computations by adapting numerical fluid dynamics concepts for the streamline simplification and acceleration of the renormalization group flow equation. This strategy involves dynamically identifying relevant directions in the parameter space based on the flow equation and its inherent stability properties. We initially examine the applicability of our approach to zero-dimensional quantum field theories, taking the $O(N)$ model as our primary example. By solving the renormalization group flow equation numerically, our results show good agreement with the theory for correlation functions and their approach to fixed points at both infrared and ultraviolet endpoints. Our analysis yields precise values for the critical exponents and fixed point locations, confirming that our method is a reliable numerical tool for studying zero-dimensional quantum field theories.

Music enthusiasts still heavily depend on conventional search engines like Google for pop music, which is surprising considering how indispensable the internet has become in everyday life. Our innovative proposal is for a music-centric search engine called Pied Piper, which will serve as a comprehensive meta-search tool, enabling users to find relevant music information by searching for lyrics, song metadata, audio, or a blend of any of these options.

This PhD research focuses on exploring specific geometric constructs over Lie groupoids and differential stacks. Key concepts, such as connections, linear connections, and semi-linear connections, have not been extensively studied in the context of Lie groupoids and stacks. Therefore, this thesis aims to bridge that knowledge gap by providing a detailed analysis of these constructs. It also identifies potential applications and areas for further research in this field.

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically those that could be linked to low-mass young stellar objects, and those connected to more massive star-forming regions.  The former group demonstrates what appears to be core shrinkage, whereas the latter exhibits core growth.  This distinction is bolstered by comparisons with nearby cores that do not have outflow signatures, and is consistent with theoretical models predicting different mass evolution paths for low-mass and high-mass young star-forming regions.  The findings suggest that core growth is a significant factor in the creation of massive star-forming regions.

Godel modal logics can be regarded as an extension of intutionistic modal logics with prelinearity. This study explores algebraic and relational semantics for Godel modal logics built upon the duality between finite Godel algebras and finite forests, a type of poset. The research considers subvarieties of basic Godel algebras with two modal operators, alongside their respective classes of forest frames, both with single and double accessibility relations. These relational structures serve as prelinear counterparts to traditional intuitionistic modal logic semantics. The study specifically examines two expansions of finite Godel algebras: the addition of Dunn axioms, common in positive classical and intutionistic logic, and the addition of Fischer Servi axioms. The research provides Jonsson-Tarski-like representation theorems for different types of finite Godel modal algebras with operators.

LiDAR point clouds offer valuable measurements for complex environmental settings, allowing for updates to digital elevation models and applications such as glacial monitoring, detecting structural changes, forest assessment, tracking shoreline and beach alterations, landslide risk analysis, habitat mapping, and urban planning. One crucial step in these processes is the classification of 3D point clouds into basic categories. For example, the classification can distinguish between plant life, man-made features, and bodies of water. Our research aims to present an initial evaluation of various classification techniques for 3D LiDAR data, including decision trees, fully connected networks, extra trees, gradient boosting, k-nearest neighbors, lightweight networks, multinomial logistic regression, multinomial naive Bayes, nested trees, random forests, and stochastic gradient boosting. This evaluation provides a starting point for further research in this area.

Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been widely utilized in various applications. These recurrences are often linked to the characteristics of a system of special functions, representing the geometric properties of the underlying space. The (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions, defined on the sphere, relies on the expansion coefficients of these functions in Gegenbauer polynomials. The recent breakthrough demonstrates the applicability of conventional differentiation and integration methods that maintain positive definiteness, although they alter the space dimension by increments of two. To address the need for a dimension increase of one, this paper creates specialized operators acting on the Gegenbauer polynomials and guaranteeing the preservation of (strict) positive definiteness.

The source of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) has remained a major puzzle in high-energy astrophysics for many years. To shed light on this enigma, researchers are correlating UHECRs with high-energy neutrinos as they offer a direct and magnetically unbiased glimpse into hadronic interactions of cosmic rays. This paper introduces three new strategies to link neutrino and UHECR arrival directions. With upgraded data sets from IceCube Neutrino Observatory and ANTARES for neutrinos, as well as from Pierre Auger Observatory and the Telescope Array for UHECRs, statistical significance and accuracy are significantly enhanced compared to the results from 2015. The analyses comprise looking for UHECR-UHECR excess around neutrino sources, searching for UHECR excess along high-energy neutrino paths, and finding UHECR-neutrino pairs on diverse scales. None of the analyses uncovered substantial deviations, thus diminishing previously reported over-statistical findings and providing tighter constraints on the spatial scales of UHECR sources.

The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements has been validated for the surface slippage and stationary regimes by referencing existing models. Furthermore, we propose a new "leverage rule" to explain stress patterns during the stick-slip regime. The occurrence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes is governed by a roughness factor that considers the relationship between the size of surface asperities and the curvature of Plateau borders.

This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine attributes and 27,045 images was utilized, with classes considered rare and normal serving as the training and validation sets, and the remaining as a test set. The approach employed to detect rare cases relied on a novel outlier detection method combining entropy and a deep learning platform, while a multi-layer perceptron was used to classify normal samples. The ensemble of 25 MLPs yielded the lowest error rate of 12.80% on the test set.

The steady-state behavior of an elastic membrane, situated between two fluids of differing densities in a rotating Hele-Shaw cell, subject to external pressure, is examined in a study that also compares its inextensibility to that of an extremely elastic membrane. When the inner fluid density surpasses the outer fluid density, the membrane exhibits a Rayleigh-Taylor-like instability caused by centrifugal force, competing with the curvature and tension-driven restorative forces, thus dictating the size of the developed finger. Numerical computation techniques are utilized to analyze not just nonlinear finger patterns but also modes with both circumferentially confined folds and branches that occur with variations in the rate of rotation and imposed pressure. Bifurcation diagrams representing a variety of pattern formations have been derived from these computations, providing a comprehensive understanding of the governing nonlinear regime.

Building on a novel theory, microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics, we've successfully applied it to examine the dynamics of systems undergoing expansion or contraction, despite a significant challenge. Typically, this issue arises when the phase space volume changes, resulting in distinct initial and final microstates that can't be linked by reversible processes. We present an innovative solution to overcome this limitation, using a system that undergoes free expansion without an external influence, and demonstrate that the proposed method aligns with thermodynamic principles. Our solution identifies the dissipated energy as a thermodynamic average of work performed by each individual microstate and confirms its nonnegative value during free expansion, which holds surprising implications.

Scientists have identified the presence of two specific isomers, 1- and 2-ethynyl-1,3-cyclopentadiene, of ethynyl cyclopentadiene (C5H5CCH) emanating from the TMC-1 direction, with column densities indicating a vast 10 to 100 times difference compared to a related cyclopropyl ring system. A possible explanation for this disparity is based on the cyclopentadiene ring's inherent instability when exposed to high energy conditions, as well as the non-equilibrium nature of interstellar environments which may favor the formation of less stable cyclopentadiene derivatives over their cyclopropyl counterparts. Detection of these ethynyl cyclopentadiene isomers also provides new insight into the interstellar production of cyanoacetylene (CCH) and the acetylenic ring system, suggesting a total CCH abundance of approximately 3.5 10 to the power of 4 per 10 to the power of 21, nearly double previous estimates.

In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks.

The significant discrepancy between advancing computational technology and real-world problem-solving led to a new field of study. Abramson and Parashar predict that similar disparities will drive the development of new computational paradigms. To support their theory, the authors draw from the history of grid computing, an example of a computational paradigm driven by a translational challenge. From a conceptual perspective, the article defines a computational paradigm as consisting of both foundational technological components and applicable domains. Before the emergence of grid computing as a paradigm, both its technology and target domains were relatively underdeveloped. The authors associate the birth of the grid computing paradigm with the intersection of two trajectories - one representing the technological aspect and the other the domain side. Based on interviews with key figures and a review of relevant documents, the article presents a detailed account of how the grid computing paradigm evolved. It highlights the crucial role of a translational approach in the grid computing story, where experts strived to bridge the gap between complex computational technologies and real-world challenges. The article also reflects on the current status and future directions of the field, concluding with the anticipation that similar conditions will give rise to new computational paradigms, driven by the extensive differences between computational technologies and practical issues to be resolved.

A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous components. This model has the ability to smoothly transition between the equations of state for dark energy and dust at different cosmological epochs, by asymptotically interpolating between two power laws. A constant viscosity coefficient underlies the model's dissipative component. Using a phase space analysis, we investigate the model's dynamics for both flat and closed universes, and through numerical computations, we determine the parameters that define the model's initial conditions. These initial conditions lead to a universe that undergoes a transition from a dust-like state in its early stages to a dark energy-like state in its present day.

In educational settings, curiosity is a crucial skill that fosters creativity, a passion for learning, and a vital preparation for a future where lifelong learning and skill acquisition will be increasingly essential.  Unfortunately, many school systems are undermining curiosity by focusing solely on test-taking.  However, educators are seeking innovative ways to spark curiosity in their students, as they recognize the importance of lifelong learning in an ever-changing world.  One understudied aspect of curiosity is its link to peer interactions.  Our study introduces a pioneering theoretical framework that combines cognitive and social factors to explain how peers can inspire curiosity through various observable behaviors and underlying states.  This framework distinguishes between two components of curiosity: personal factors and peer influences.  Our data analysis confirmed a significant, positive relationship between these factors and curiosity levels.  Additionally, our results highlighted key behaviors that contribute to curiosity in learning environments.  Building on these findings, we developed practical strategies that can be incorporated into learning technologies to identify, stimulate, and guide curiosity in real-time.  Our work is a significant step towards designing more effective learning technologies that recognize and respond to curiosity in collaborative learning settings and also paves the way for the development of computer support for other important cognitive and emotional skills.

Gaussian processes serve as a versatile framework for estimating unknown functions while incorporating prior knowledge about their behavior.  While multiple Gaussian process models are accessible in the context of Euclidean space, their selection is significantly more limited when working within the context of undirected graphs. This research adapts the stochastic partial differential equation formulation for Mat\'ern Gaussian processes - commonly employed in spatial regression - such that it may be applied to various graph domains, including random field and social network graphs.  We demonstrate the benefits of this adaptation by comparing its performance against alternative Gaussian process models on synthetic and real-world data sets.

The effective management of urban roads plays a crucial role in the optimal operation of urban transportation systems and overall city functioning. Current monitoring techniques rely heavily on inductive loop sensors, roadside cameras, and crowdsourced data, but they often come with limitations of high costs, restricted coverage areas, or unreliable data due to low user participation rates. In this study, a groundbreaking approach of mobile sensing is presented, utilizing a large fleet of ridesharing vehicles to monitor and interpret the condition of urban roads as they traverse through the network. Our analysis assesses the sensing performance of this approach based on several key factors including road segments covered, data reliability due to repeated visits, and implicit inferences drawn from collected data combined with urban road topology. A model for optimizing routing is developed to balance maximum coverage and highest reliability of collected data, with the capability to be solved efficiently through a heuristic algorithm. Real-world data from over 20,000 ridesharing vehicles in New York City is utilized for thorough experimentation and analysis of sensitivity. Our results show significant advancements in road coverage and reliability improvement through this approach, achieving an overall increase of at least 13% in covered road segments and a reduction of at least 11% in unreliable data with respect to a baseline system.

Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We examined how sensitive the existing J/ψ decay width and muon $(g-2)_\mu$ measurements constraints are to various neutrino and dark matter parameters when taking into account hadronic corrections and radiative contributions from these particles. We discovered that the current J/ψ invisible width limits, when considering a 0.39 eV^2 mass scale for a light sterile neutrinity or a 10^-9 dm^2 mass scale for a sub-GeV dark matter particle, are already near their sensitivity threshold. Furthermore, we found that a 0.29 eV^2 mass scale for a light sterile neutrinity or a 10^-9 dm^2 mass scale for a sub-GeV dark matter particle could be constrained to a 0.39 eV^2 or 0.29 eV^2 mass scale for a light sterile neutrinity or a 10^-9 dm^2 mass scale for a sub-GeV dark matter particle could be constrained to a factor of 10-20 times better than the existing J/ψ decay width constraints. Moreover, we found that a 0.29 eV^2 mass scale for a light sterile neutrinity

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the Nordsieck technique, and we extend this work by directly introducing variable stepsize SGLMs onto non-uniform grids. We then establish order conditions for these new methods of order p with q=p stage order and demonstrate them through specific examples up to order four, further confirming their efficiency in solving non-stiff problems via numerical experiments and theoretical convergence analysis.

This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a comprehensive framework consisting of theoretical underpinnings and a step-by-step implementation guide for the algorithm. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of MFSSA through comparative studies of reconstruction accuracy in multivariate functional time series (MFTS) and real-world applications, including the analysis of intraday temperature curves and remote sensing images of vegetation. Additionally, MFSSA is made available through the Rfssa R package for user convenience.

Deep learning-based automated essay scoring systems are increasingly employed by educational institutions and testing agencies to evaluate numerous applicants, making critical decisions in the process. Yet, surprisingly little research has focused on comprehending how these models function and identifying potential weaknesses. This study reveals a significant issue with contemporary models, revealing that they are prone to sudden changes in scoring patterns in response to minor alterations in essay content, a phenomenon known as "over-sensitivity." Furthermore, our analysis exposes inherent biases in these models, which can result in inconsistent interpretations of the same input. To address this concern, we present two distinct approachs aimed at mitigating the over-sensitivity and bias of these models, which have shown a marked improvement in performance in preliminary evaluations.

The power law decay $p(t,x) \sim t^{-\phi(x,b)/2}$ holds, where $p(t,x)$ is the probability that, during the interval $[1,t]$, the random walk $S$ with zero-mean increments has spent a fraction of time greater than $x$ with non-negative values, occurring for a walk that is defined by finitely many i.i.d. increment values. The parameter $\phi(x,b)$ is determined by the probability $\mathbb{P}(\text{L\'evy}(1/2,\kappa(x,b))<0)$ where $\kappa(x,b) = \frac{\sqrt{1-x}b-\sqrt{1+x}}{\sqrt{1-x}b+\sqrt{1+x}}$ with $b = b_S \geq 0$ indicating the relative magnitude between positive and negative excursions of the random walk.

The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A new plasma source, specifically a helicon-type source, was installed at IShTAR to replicate the plasma conditions found in an ITER-like device. A key aspect of this source is understanding the plasma within it requires analysis beyond basic parameters such as density and temperature. Additionally, it must be confirmed that the plasma source operates in helicon mode. This study presents the results of analyzing plasma emissions from IShTAR with a focus on these aspects. It reveals that both a high-frequency interferometer and a spectral analysis of plasma emissions confirm that the plasma density in the source is in the range expected for a helicon source and follows the characteristic decreasing trend along the magnetic field lines consistent with helicon mode. It also includes a comparison with existing sources and an assessment of the limitations inherent in using spectral analysis on such a large scale.

In comparison to conventional chemical pesticides, microbial pesticides exhibit numerous advantages, which can be modelled through a system where entomopathogenic nematodes are used to eliminate and concurrently suppress the population of target insects. This system aims to manage pests through a continuous nematode release mechanism, where the model's equilibrium and Hopf bifurcation periodic solutions are analyzed for optimal pest control, which is further confirmed by numerical simulations and case studies.

While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers commonly employ strategies such as increasing the resolution of images, introducing constraints based on 3D geometry, and using auxiliary masks. However, these methods are usually application-specific and do not generalize well to other tasks. In an effort to create more versatile and easily adaptable models for nucleus segmentation, the author of this paper proposes a novel approach called the W-Net model, which combines a segmentation network with a matching network to match segmented regions with the corresponding areas in the image. By conducting experiments on colon and liver cell segmentation, the author demonstrates that the W-Net model outperforms traditional WLS-based methods and shows a notable improvement in processing images with adherent nuclei.

Let's consider a non-Archimedean local field of characteristic not two and denote it by F. Additionally, let G be either a specific type of special orthogonal group with an odd number of dimensions or a symplectic group with a specific dimensionality, denoted as SO(2r+1)(F) or Sp(2r)(F) respectively. This paper focuses on establishing the local converse theorem for the representation of G. To this end, for two given irreducible admissible generic representations of G, with shared central character and gamma factors, our result stipulates that these representations are isomorphic. To prove this, we draw from the Cogdell, Shahidi, and Tsai framework of partial Bessel functions and the categorization of irreducible generic representations. Furthermore, our result extends the earlier works by Jiang and Soudry as well as Q. Zhang, by expanding on their results for the cases with supercuspidal representations in a wider set of characteristic settings.

Xiong and Liu previously provided a definition for graphs G that have hamiltonian n-th iterated line graphs, L^n(G), where n is 2 or greater. In this study, we examine whether an L^n(G) graph possesses a hamiltonian path, and offer a definition for G to achieve this condition. Additionally, we apply this definition to set multiple upper limits for a graph's hamiltonian path index.

Cell death due to pyroptosis, characterized by inflammation, can contribute to the high cytokine levels seen in severe cases of COVID-19.  Pyroptosis is primarily initiated through the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation which can be triggered by SARS-CoV-2 infection. Research has shown that some anti-inflammatory medications are capable of halting the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, thereby delaying pyroptotic cell death. Our study develops a single-cell mathematical model to analyze the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, cell death due to pyroptosis, and how these processes respond to treatment. Formulated in terms of system dynamics and stochasticity at the single-cell level, the model examines the effects of intervention on pyroptosis and inflammation. Analyzing this model provides insights into immune system dynamics and how they are affected by intervention, and it also paves the way for further exploration of host-pathogen interactions.

External influences affecting states and reward signals can hinder reinforcement learning by introducing unanticipated fluctuations in the reward signal. This concept is mathematically formalized, and the conditions are identified under which an environment involving uncontrollable state variables can be broken down into two separate components: an environment solely affected by the uncontrollable state and reward variables, and an environment defined by the variables that can be controlled. Additionally, a condition for reducing the complexity of these variables in Monte Carlo policy evaluation is established, leading to potential acceleration of this process. This acceleration could be applied across a broader range of reinforcement learning algorithms. Two methods are devised for identifying the uncontrollable state variables, and the results from applying these methods to multiple test environments show a notable increase in efficiency and a potential for speeding up the reinforcement learning process.

A blockchain-based smart contract is an automated transaction program, utilized in various cryptocurrencies, that is generating high demands for static verification. To fulfill this need, our project HELMHOLTZ is introduced in this article as a static verification tool specifically designed for Michelson, a statically-typed programming language used in the Tezos blockchain. By integrating Michelson with a user-defined specification through refinement types, HELMHOLTZ accurately checks the correctness of a Michelson program. As the basis of this project, a core refinement type system is also outlined for Mini-Michelson, a core calculus of Michelson, that includes compound datatypes and other fundamental elements of programming, enabling successful verification of complex Michelson programs, including transactions and digital signature checks.

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases. A numerical example serves to guide readers visually and numerically through each step of the GCNN process.

In a three-dimensional spacetime, Einstein's gravity theory is transformed to represent a scalar field with a complex, self-correcting mechanism. The field's behavior can be reinterpreted using Chern-Simons form for a group of symmetries known as $g^{+}\oplus g^{-}$, depending on specific parameters that either support $so(2,2)$, $so(3,1)$ or $iso(2,1)$ symmetries. The resulting equations of motion for this system are then described as non-flat connections, from which conserved charges can be deduced using established formulas, albeit those of standard Chern-Simons theory. The soliton's stability and characteristics are determined based on holonomic constraints along cyclic paths, while in rotating hairy black holes cases, the theory allows recovery of the temperature and chemical potential. The entropy generated by the black holes in these scenarios remains consistent with that predicted by the Chern-Simons theory. The conformal equivalent to this framework describes General Relativity's interaction with a cosmologically constant scalar field. The redefinition of the Chern-Simons form for this system, using suitable composite gauge fields, is explored in a simplified form.

Theories of supersymmetric Yang-Mills with algebra so(4N) can have non-trivial, invertible-defying symmetries. By utilizing holographic duality, we can determine the branes equivalent to these symmetries, and deduce the fusion principles for the symmetries through brane dynamics.

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies on precise measurement of tissue displacement in multiple directions. Notwithstanding advancements in elastography, axial displacement estimation outperforms lateral displacement estimation due to increased sampling rate, higher resolution, and the carrier signal's axial propagation. The synthetic aperture (SA) ultrasound technique boasts better lateral resolution than its counterparts; however, its limited imaging depth restricts its elastography applications. The virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) technique bridges this limitation by integrating SA with focused transmitted data while maintaining the same high lateral resolution. Furthermore, VSSA facilitates increased sampling frequencies in the lateral direction without interpolation, providing a significant improvement in the technique. This study leverages VSSA to enhance beamforming, achieving increased lateral resolution and sampling frequencies, and employs the recently introduced elastography technique, OVERWIND, for data analysis. Simulation and experimental outcomes reveal notable enhancements in the estimation of lateral tissue displacement.

Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. This approach can be seen as a natural extension to the concept of a computability logic web, but now incorporating the capacity for forward reasoning.

The concept of Boolean Ramsey numbers for sets of posets was initially explored in relation to Boolean lattices and posets obtained from chains with minimal elements combined into a V-shaped structure. A key objective is to establish a minimum number 'n' for any number of color options where a given V-shaped poset will be entirely colored with a specific color in a Boolean lattice. Recent work has led to the determination of Boolean Ramsey numbers for certain instances, and this paper aims to build on that by investigating the same concept for V-shaped posets and identifying minimum posets containing the Ramsey property in Boolean lattices of a particular size. Another area of research within this paper focuses on Boolean rainbow Ramsey numbers which involve identifying either a monochromatic structure or a structure with different color components within a Boolean lattice. This study explores this concept for V-shaped posets and their antichains.

In the context of dynamic data streams, where Euclidean space points are added or removed from a dataset, we develop a one-pass coreset algorithm for solving the $k$-means clustering problem. Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, making it the first algorithm for this problem to utilize dimension-dependent storage while maintaining linear dependence on the target center count $k$.

We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing the outcome values of the individual games as rewards in the aggregated framework. Through extensive simulations, our hierarchical model demonstrates substantial computational efficiency improvements while achieving comparable performance to flat Nash policies.

Inspired by classic counterintuitive phenomena, a particular n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ within the range [0,1] is classified as 'cyclic' when there exist unique, independent random variables $(U_1, \ldots, U_n)$ where the likelihood of $U_{i+1}$ being greater than $U_i$ is $x_i$ for $i$ ranging from 1 to n-1, and the likelihood of $U_1$ being greater than $U_n$ is $x_n$. If this condition, combined with the additional stipulation that all individual elements $x_i$ be greater than 0.5, is satisfied, the n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ is classified as 'nontransitive'. 

We represent the likelihood of selecting a random n-tuple that meets these 'cyclic' criteria as $p_n$ and its 'nontransitive' counterpart as $p_n^*$. In our analysis, we find the exact values of $p_3$ and $p_3^*$, and establish upper and lower limits for $p_n$ in instances where n is 4 or greater, indicating a probability approaching 1 as n increases without bound. Our research also identifies the specific probability distribution associated with the smallest, central, and largest components in a 'cyclic' triple.

Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, particularly due to their impressive performance at a relatively low computational cost. A key method in this area, the unsupervised cycleGAN approach, has demonstrated great promise in upgrading the quality of low-dose images without needing matched high-dose images as reference data. However, the use of two neural network generators in the training process is a significant limitation, primarily because the extra generator adds complexity and memory demands. In response to these issues, we have introduced a new cycleGAN framework based on a single, adaptive switchable generator. By incorporating adaptive instance normalization (AdaIN) layers, the baseline generator can efficiently transform a low-dose CT image into a routine-dose CT image and then easily switch to generating high-dose images from low-dose images simply by modifying the AdaIN codes. The proposed architecture achieves these conversions while minimizing the memory requirement and weight increase associated with additional generators, and can therefore be trained with more stability using limited training data. Our results demonstrate that the new method not only rivals but outperforms previous cycleGAN methods while needing only roughly half as many parameters.

Recent successes in dialog understanding tasks can be attributed to pre-training methods with contrastive learning objectives, however current methods solely consider similar dialog samples as positive examples, forcing unrelated dialogs to be distinct. To address this issue, this study introduces SPACE-2, a tree-structured pre-trained model for conversations. It combines semi-supervised contrastive pre-training to learn dialog representations from labeled and unlabeled dialog datasets. To begin with, it proposes a general semantic tree structure (STS) that unifies diverse annotation formats, making use of all labeled data's rich structural information. Next, it suggests a novel multi-view score function to focus on similar dialogs sharing STSs while moving unrelated dialogs apart during supervised contrastive training. To maximize unlabeled dialogs' potential, it incorporates a self-supervised contrastive loss to refine the learned representations. Experimental results show SPACE-2 achieves top-notch performance across seven datasets on four dialog understanding tasks in the DialoGLUE benchmark. The model's code and data can be found at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/DAMO-ConvAI/tree/main/space-2 for reproducibility purposes.

This research aims to examine the geometric makeup of an ideal fluid's spacetime 
when coupled with a torsion-forming vector field and the relationship between the 
conformal Ricci-Yamabe metric and the conformal eta-Ricci-Yamabe metric. We first 
derive conditions for the conformal Ricci-Yamabe soliton to be in a state of 
expansion, stability, or contraction. Subsequently, we establish Laplace's 
equation in the context of an ideal fluid's spacetime when coupled with a 
conservative vector field and determine its relationship to the conformal 
eta-Ricci-Yamabe soliton.

To study the rotational characteristics of distorted halos, we utilized the angular momentum projection method on wave functions derived from the deformed relativistic Hartree-Bogoliubov theory in continuum. Our self-consistent approach effectively accounts for interactions between single particle bound states and the continuum across ground and rotational states. By analyzing rotational states in isotopes of $^{42}$Mg and $^{44}$Mg, specifically excitation energy, configuration, and density distribution, our research demonstrates that deformed halo structures endure from intrinsic ground states to collective rotational states, particularly illustrating shape decoupling effects in rotating distorted halo nuclei.

A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent structure, with the BasicVSR method being one of the top-performing frameworks, leveraging bidirectional propagation and feature alignment to utilize information from the input video. In our research, we upgrade BasicVSR by incorporating second-order grid propagation and a deformable alignment guided by optical flow, enabling the efficient exploitation of spatial and temporal information across misaligned frames. Our enhanced model, BasicVSR++, significantly outperforms the original by achieving a notable improvement in PSNR, with only a minimal increase in computational cost. Moreover, our model exhibits versatility in video restoration tasks and achieved remarkable success in video super-resolution and compressed video enhancement challenges in NTIRE 2021, earning several top ranks, with codes and models available on MMEditing.

Due to the tendency for high-energy lepton colliders to radiate forward and resemble weak boson colliders beyond a few TeV, a new perspective is taken that treats weak bosons as fundamental components of these leptons. Within this context of a muon collider, we evaluate the relevance of W and Z particle distribution functions, particularly at their leading order in 2-to-n particle interactions. A thorough examination of both universal and near-universal adjustments, specifically power-law and logarithmic corrections, is carried out to determine the derivation of (polarized) weak boson distribution functions when approaching a limit of collinearity. A survey is also conducted to analyze multiple 2-to-n particle interactions at 2-to-30 TeV energy levels through weak boson fusion/scattering in both polarized and unpolarized conditions. A key contribution of this study involves the public integration of Effective W/Z and Weizs\"acker-Williams Approximations, collectively referred to as the Effective Vector Boson Approximation, into the existing event generator software MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO, setting the groundwork for developing matching prescriptions between EW parton showers and EW distribution functions, and providing actionable advice on the use of W/Z PDFs to facilitate this development.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios.

The paper provides derivations of Li-Yau and Souplet-Zhang type estimates for the equation $u_t=\Delta_\xi p + \lambda u + A(u)$ in a complete, non-compact metric measure space with compact boundary. Furthermore, the paper includes local gradient estimates for the equation $\Delta_\xi(u^p)+\lambda u + A(u) = 0$ on complete, non-compact manifolds with compact boundary.

We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a modified version of Godel's Second Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, demonstrating how these results collectively imply the unsatisfiability of any consistent, formal theory's consistency statement.

This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space.

When the population is not fully known in advance, sampling occurs in sequence, either individually or in batches, which are obtained sequentially. This work presents a novel algorithm that allows for sequential selection of a balanced sample. The algorithm accommodates equal and unequal inclusion probabilities and can also be applied to select spatially balanced samples when the population contains geographical coordinates. Moreover, an investigation using simulated data reveals that the proposed method surpasses alternative methods.

In robotics, calibrating an eye-in-hand camera using image information is an essential task that has been extensively researched. We investigated using artificial intelligence-based methods for this purpose by leveraging only a single color image, utilizing exclusively simulated data to train the models. Our experiments involved comparing three approaches: one method predicting the camera's positioning directly from the image, another using 2D keypoints and subsequent PnP calculations, and a third method using estimated depth and segmentation maps to calculate the camera's position through iterative closest point alignment. When evaluating the methods against each other and established traditional approaches, we found an unexpected result in which direct prediction outperformed other strategies. Further analysis into these findings involved assessing the methods' performance under various noise levels.

In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography and deblurring. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the data and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. We developed a method to generate a multitude of high-quality samples per second from the posterior distribution by using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which outperformed current methods according to Fr\'{e}chet inception distance metrics in applications like MRI with multiple coils and image deblurring.

This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions for specific invariant configurations in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. We also discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds.

Next-generation wireless networks require exceptionally high data transfer rates that could be achieved by utilizing Terahertz frequency bands for communication. Traditionally, THz communication is confined to short-distance applications because THz signals face high absorption in the atmosphere. To overcome this limitation, researchers have explored the potential of multi-hop directional transmission techniques to extend communication range, albeit these schemes can result in prolonged beam training time using conventional methods such as exhaustive search or hierarchical approaches. To tackle this problem, a novel hierarchical beam training technique is proposed in this paper that dynamically optimizes training levels across individual single-hop links, maximizing overall spectral efficiency. To tackle this optimization problem in the presence of channel state uncertainty and noise, a reinforcement learning solution inspired by the multi-armed bandit problem is proposed. Simulations show the new technique converges quickly in dynamic channel conditions and offers up to 75% better performance than conventional methods in terms of spectral efficiency.

The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components in speech and music. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given pitch values by incorporating pitch-dependent dilated convolution layers, effectively leveraging network parameters informed by musical notes. Secondly, additional residual networks are employed with cycle consistency loss to enforce periodic signal constraints within specific time frames, enabling the model to learn implicit periodic coefficients. Experimental evaluations of QPNet on speech and music datasets reveal superior results, outperforming the original WaveNet in terms of frequency spectrogram similarity and listening tests.

This research presents a novel annotation and correction tool for Arabic texts,
namely MADARi, catering to Standard and Dialectal varieties. MADARi offers a user-
friendly interface and efficient management capabilities for annotating and handling
a considerable volume of texts. Its key features encompass a range of morphological
annotations, such as identifying the base form of words, associated clitics, part of
speech, lemma, translation, and dialect-specific markers. To facilitate productivity,
MADARi offers a set of built-in tools, including precomputed analysis to guide
annotators, access to multiple dialects via morphological analyzers, and retrieval
of prior annotations. Additionally, MADARi enables lead annotators to supervise and
coordinate the annotation process in a distributed and concurrent manner. We delve
into the rationale, design, and execution of this interface and present results from
an experiment conducted with the system.

Planets similar to Earth, orbiting nearby stars with reduced energy output, are being extensively studied and several are suited for further analysis. Focusing on temperate worlds surrounded by thick H2 atmospheres, our models follow chemical transformations and gas circulation after H2O, CH4, NH3, and H2S molecules break apart under stellar radiation, utilizing K2-18 b, PH2 b, and Kepler-167 e as prime examples. According to our simulations, NH3 molecules are destroyed by solar radiation in atmospheres surrounding G/K stars, while intact in those surrounding M stars. Typically, NH3 breaks down in presence of H2O, forming H2O-NH3 complexes, while CH4 and H2S remain separate entities. Their relative abundance is defined by various parameters, including the altitude at which the atmosphere starts absorbing stellar radiation, system solar luminosity, and the number of molecules surrounding the exoplanet. These factors influence the spectral unique fingerprint of each exoplanet, as modelled through their infrared and visible light spectra.

To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and those from other causes at non-zero temperatures, our method involves swapping the normal lead in tunneling spectroscopy with a high-resistance lead (characterized by large Ohm values). The increased resistance in this setup significantly alters tunneling conductance, impacting it in distinct ways. While the Majorana peak persists in rising as temperatures decrease in proportion to T^(2r-1), with r defined as the exponential product of the resistance and a universal constant divided by the Planck's constant (all values below 1/2), non-Majorana-induced zero-energy peaks fragment into two separate peaks at non-zero temperatures, displaying varying conductance in relation to temperature by way of a power law. Furthermore, tunneling associated with a Majorana mode falls within the same broad class of universal behaviors as does the case for unstable critical points with a non-Majorana mode.

The development of advanced detection algorithms through deep learning has accelerated the identification of road issues, including automatic defect detection and marking analysis. To expedite and reduce costs associated with manual inspections, a comprehensive system called RoadAtlas has been developed, providing a holistic solution encompassing road flaw detection, marking parsing, interactive data visualization through a web interface, and a robust database framework supported by API tools.

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence.

Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically extracts challenging samples and incorporates them into a contrastive learning framework. Our algorithm achieves superior results on the Flickr SoundNet dataset, a prominent benchmark. Moreover, we introduce a new dataset called VGG-Sound Source, a comprehensive set of annotated video clips featuring sound sources with explicit bounding box markings. VGG-Sound Source surpasses existing datasets in scale, size, and category diversity, consisting of 5,000 videos spanning over 200 categories. Notably, it differs from Flickr SoundNet in that it is based on video data. Our algorithm also demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on this new dataset when compared to several baseline methods.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion.

This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequality and a compactness-uniqueness argument. An operator theoretical approach provides the regularity needed for initial conditions, thereby obtaining the desired stability estimate.

A new method has been created that successfully transfers squeezed states into optical cavities even in stable conditions. The method builds upon conventional optomechanical setups, utilizing a three-level atom to facilitate the transfer. Two techniques were devised to observe the squeezed state transfer effect, including applying a controlled influx of squeezed phonons and simulating the system in an environment of phonon-squeezed vibrations. Our model demonstrates that in an ideal setup, the optical cavity will reflect phonon-squeezed states, resulting in the emergence of squeezed coherent states. Notably, this phenomenon endures even in a closed system, allowing for the continuous generation of squeezed states. We also explored the conditions required for this transfer by varying key system parameters and found that it can be achieved with optomechanical interactions as weak as $g_{om} = 0.1\gamma$, where $\gamma$ is the decay rate of the optical mode.

We examine an expansion of modal $\mu$-calculus, specifically considering its application to sets comprised of fundamental elements and investigate its core properties. The complexity of model verification can be resolved for orbit-finite structures, and a parallel connection with parity games exists. In contrast, the issue of determining satisfaction becomes insoluble. Additionally, the limitations of modal $\mu$-calculi with enriched atoms are identified, and we explore how the expressive potential of these systems depends on both the arrangement of these atoms and whether a basic or composite syntax is employed.

We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating
variations in impulsivity, which is analogous to the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting
model proposed by Takahashi, with a dual nature. We show that our model's
parameters correlate with the average and standard deviation of impulsivity, and
these results provide a clear path for investigating the Tsallis distribution in a
social context.

When considering linearized gravity within a harmonic gauge theory for a symmetric tensor field, implementing the harmonic gauge yields multiple gauge options, resulting in the gauge appearing as a class rather than a singular choice.  This feature provides a physical justification for adopting a specific covariant harmonic gauge that arises when a mass term is added to the gravitational perturbation.  Specifically, one particular choice of harmonic gauge leads to a linearized massive gravity model with the correct five degrees of freedom and avoids vDVZ discontinuity, in contrast to the standard Fierz-Pauli theory.

A signed graph is created by adding a polarity to the edges of an existing graph, and this concept of signed graphs has recently been integrated with other graph theory ideas like minors and coloring. By examining the notion of Extended Double Covers, recently proposed by researchers, this work delves deeper into understanding the relationships between planar signed graphs and their connections to the Four-Color Theorem. The authors present a new conjecture, stating that certain graphs which allow homomorphisms to any planar signed graph, will themselves also be able to receive homomorphisms to any planar signed graph, and then prove a related theorem for a certain subclass of graphs without a K_4 minor, and explore near optimal bounds for other subclasses. Additionally, this work introduces the idea of assigning weights to the polarity of edges in a graph, expanding the definition of a signed graph.

For a class of quadratic Hamiltonians, a transformation of Weyl-Wigner symbols through a change of variables reveals the canonical thermal equilibrium quantum states, using the Weyl-Wigner representations and metaplectic operators, whose associated unitary classical structures behave predictably under the transformation, exposing the complex symplectic matrix that dictates the entire thermal equilibrium state and thereby determines its thermal properties. Additionally, a thorough examination is performed of four distinct types of Hamiltonian dynamics: parabolic, elliptic, hyperbolic, and loxodromic dynamics. Semiclassical and high-temperature approximations are both determined and contrasted to their respective classical or quadratic behaviors.

The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both mathematical and graphical means, specifically in the context of a two-level system. We contend that the simplicity of these calculations can offer undergraduates a clear, tangible understanding of the concept of negative absolute temperature.

Let G be an abelian group and A a nonempty subset of G, with elements indexed as $a_0, a_1,..., a_{k-1}$. For any positive integer h less than or equal to k, we can calculate a restricted signed sumset denoted as $h\hat{}_{\underline{+}}A$, which comprises sums of $a_i$ with weights from {-1,0,1}. The goal of this article is to solve the minimum value of $|h\hat{}_{\underline{+}}A|$, where $|A|$, when A is a set of integers, and investigate the underlying structure of A to achieve this minimum value. Additionally, some open questions related to $h\hat{}_{\underline{+}}A$ are proposed in this article.

Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. The process of polyp characterization involves examining tissue samples for malignancy and dysplasia using histological features. Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved medical pattern recognition accuracy; however, training these models necessitates vast collections of annotated medical images. In this context, we've developed UniToPatho, an extensive dataset consisting of 9536 annotated H&E stained patches derived from 292 whole-slide images, designed for deep learning-based classification and grading of colorectal polyps and adenomas. This dataset serves as a resource for researchers tackling the complex task of automating colorectal polyp characterization.

A novel numerical approach has been introduced for solving time-harmonic acoustic scattering issues, primarily centered around analyzing the impact of smoothly varying material inhomogeneities on plane waves. This method's efficiency is optimal for high-frequency scenarios and is adaptable across any given frequency $\omega$. The approach operates within a time-domain framework, consisting of three main components: generating a suitable incoming plane wave with compact propagation direction, solving the time-domain scattering problem, and ultimately deriving the time-harmonic solution via Fourier transformation. Crucial to this approach is a dynamic front-tracking mesh adaptation technique which minimizes the required computational degrees of freedom, thereby enhancing performance by limiting support to the wave front's spatial extent. To complement this strategy, an alternative Fourier transformation method is developed, taking advantage of the optimized mesh dimensions to provide even better results. Successful applications and examples highlight the method's efficiency and adaptability with various sources, including external points and soft-scattering scenarios. However, it should be noted that trapping modes significantly reduce the method's efficiency.

We analyzed the isotopic composition of hydrogen and water content in pyroxene minerals from recent chondrite falls in Benenitra (2018) and Chelyabinsk (2013), as well as three older chondrite finds in Antarctica. In contrast to the water-rich Antarctic samples with terrestrial contamination, Benenitra and Chelyabinsk pyroxene minerals showed lower levels of water (around 0.018-0.087 wt.$\%$ H$_2$O) and D-poor isotopic signatures, ranging from -444 to -49. Evaluating these results in the context of various planetary material exchange theories, we found that they align with the outcomes of recent astrophysical simulations. These simulations suggest that there were multiple small-scale accretion events of dry inner solar system materials on the surface of Benenitra and Chelyabinsk parent asteroids. This conclusion is also supported by the presence of metal-rich CAI inclusions within these pyroxene grains, which provides further evidence for these collisions. Additionally, we found that the water content in Benenitra and Chelyabinsk pyroxene minerals can be explained by the preservation of a significant amount of water in their parent asteroid, likely originating from a late stage solar nebula or the inner solar system during the final stages of planet formation in the solar system.

Using the algebraic Bethe-ansatz method, we find exact expressions for scalar products and form factors of higher-spin XXZ chains. This applies to any spin values and mixtures thereof. We verify the affine quantum-group symmetry, $U_q(\hat{sl_2})$, for the XXZ chain's monodromy matrix, enabling exact derivation. Specifically, we use quantum-group symmetry to explicitly obtain diagonalized forms for the B and C operators within the F-basis of the spin-1/2 XXZ chain. This achievement substantiates prior conjectures about the algebraic Bethe-ansatz's correlation function calculations. These results provide a crucial foundation for systematic studies of form factors and correlation functions across solvable models connected to integrable XXZ spin chains.

Speech to text translation is the process of converting spoken language into a written foreign language. Current translation systems are typically paired with recorded audio of the source language. We are working to add a new component to these systems that can understand spoken language with no prior training and produce written text in a different language. We will also be translating spoken language to a different dialect of the same language. This new skill will be added to a speech recognition system without needing to update the underlying audio to text system. We will also be providing data to these models in the form of paired audio and text, as well as text alone. We will be testing these models on a range of translation tasks.

We assess the applicability of three different methods for calculating electromagnetic multipoles: Cartesian primitive multipoles, irreducible multipoles and spherical multipoles. Our findings suggest that the spherical multipoles provide the most accurate description of electromagnetic scattering behavior, as demonstrated with an example of an amorphous silicon sphere. These multipoles are utilized to model the optical force exerted on particles composed of semiconductors, dielectrics, and metals over a broad range of wavelengths spanning from the dipolar regime down to the Mie regime.

This study introduces two categories of elements in the algebra U(gl(n)), specifically double Young-Capelli bitableaux and central Schur elements, both displaying remarkable action on the highest weight vectors of irreducible Schur modules. The central Schur elements can be viewed as a sum of double Young-Capelli bitableaux corresponding to various strictly increasing Young tableaux. These elements equate to preimages under the Harish-Chandra isomorphism of shifted Schur polynomials, aligning with quantum immanants as per Okounkov. Notably, the representation of Schur elements/quantum immanants bypasses reliance on irreducible characters of symmetric groups. Column and row Schur elements correspond to Capelli and Nazarov-Umeda elements, with duality within these categories stemming from dual combinatorial descriptions of their eigenvalues.
